Where the Site Falls Behind

Where a Crypto Marketing Site Falls Behind the Market

The ProblemStandard Agency

The listing is announced before the page exists

A new market or token goes live on the exchange and in the community before the marketing site mentions it. The page that should carry the announcement is waiting in a ticket queue behind product work, and traders read about it somewhere else.

Engineering owns a site it never asked for

The marketing site sits in the same repository and release process as the product. Every copy change waits for a deploy window, and every campaign page costs an engineer a day the roadmap had already spent.

Regulatory wording drifts out of date by region

What the site may say about a product differs by jurisdiction and changes with each new rule. When updates take days, one region's page carries wording the compliance team retired last week, and nobody notices until a regulator does.

The SolutionThe Legency Approach

Listing pages go live inside an agreed turnaround

Requests go into a shared channel with the person doing the build. Standard requests are answered within one business day and urgent work is turned around before the day is out, so the page is up when the announcement goes out.

The marketing site comes off the product team's plate

The site runs on Webflow with a component system the marketing team publishes from, separate from the product release cycle. Engineers stop fielding copy changes, and the roadmap keeps the people it was planned around.

Compliance wording changes in one place per region

Disclosures, risk warnings and eligibility text are held as shared content, so a rule change in one jurisdiction is a single edit that updates every page carrying it. Staging comes first, so the compliance owner signs off before publish.

Built for the Category

Four Things a Crypto Engagement Delivers

A Named Owner for the Marketing Site

One accountable partner runs the Webflow site as a standing service, with a committed turnaround in a shared channel, so nobody on the product team is the fallback when a page needs to change.

Campaign Pages Built From One Pattern

Trading competitions, incentive programmes and referral drives each get a page built from the same pattern, pointed at that campaign's own data and shipped to staging first, so campaigns never cross.

Split Testing on a Standing Cycle

Tests run through Webflow Optimize one section at a time, with the build, the monitoring, the result and a recommendation for the next test, so the team always knows what to try on the page next.

A Site Kept Light Under Load

Asset weight, bandwidth and plan limits are watched as part of the service, so a listing day or an airdrop announcement is served as a normal day and never becomes an incident for engineering.

The Site as Infrastructure

A Marketing Site Judged on Uptime and Asset Weight

Crypto teams read a website the way they read a node: does it stay up, how heavy is it, what does the plan cap. The marketing site is part of the technical estate, and it is run as one.

Asset weight kept in check

Hero video, token logos and chart images add up fast. Every asset is compressed and sized before it ships, so the page stays quick on a phone for a trader checking a market between meetings.

Plan limits watched ahead of each launch

Bandwidth, CMS item counts and form submissions all have ceilings on a Webflow plan. They are tracked as part of the service, so a growing list of markets or a viral campaign does not hit a cap unannounced.

Staging before every publish

Every change ships to staging first and goes live on approval. A campaign page is checked against its own data before a trader sees it, and each campaign stays isolated so competitions never cross.

A change record engineering can read

Who changed what, and when, is recorded for every request in the shared channel. When a page moves and someone asks why, the answer exists, with a date and the person who made it.

When the Market Moves

The Site Changes the Hour the Market Does

A listing, a new market, a delisting or a regulatory notice each need the site to say something different within hours. The service is built around that cadence, with the same shared channel carrying all of it.

Listings and markets

A new market gets its page, its navigation entry and its announcement banner in one request. A delisting removes them in one request, with redirects in place so search traffic still lands on a live page.

Campaigns and competitions

Each trading competition reuses the same self-serve claim pattern: build the page, point it at that campaign's reward data, ship to staging first. A trader enters a wallet address, gets an instant eligibility answer, and every claim is logged automatically.

Regulatory notices by region

When a regulator in one jurisdiction changes what may be said about a product, the wording for that region is updated once and every page carrying it follows. Pages for every other region stay as they were.

Case Study

Working with dYdX since 2025.

dYdX runs a decentralized crypto exchange whose markets trade around the clock. Its Webflow development moved to us in 2025 and has run continuously since: urgent fixes turned around the same day, a standing split-testing programme through Webflow Optimize, and a self-serve rewards claim page for every trading competition. The relationship has since continued into a new engagement with Arcus.
